subtype: Different ways of relating in toddlerhood [Actor]
passage: Monday. Jahnavi, two, lines up her mother's steel spoons on the kitchen floor, handles all one way. When Reena calls her name, Jahnavi keeps lining. Thursday. The school bus takes a new road. Jahnavi screams and arches all the way home. Reena rocks her in the dim bedroom until she calms. Next Tuesday. Reena tells the paediatrician what she has noticed. That night Jahnavi brings her the spoons one by one, then presses her forehead to Reena's knee.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi line up on the kitchen floor?
qa.a: Her mother's steel spoons, with the handles all one way.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi pressing her forehead to Reena's knee suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels close to her mother and is showing love in her own way, after sharing the spoons she cares about.

qa.q: When the bus took a new road, what choice helped Jahnavi settle?
qa.a: Reena rocked her in the dim bedroom until she calmed; a calm, quiet place helped more than pushing her to stop.

qa.q: What might it be like for Reena when Jahnavi does not turn at her name?
qa.a: It may worry or sting at first, but the spoon gift shows Reena that Jahnavi does connect with her, just differently.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler who lines up objects, responds less to her name, is upset by a changed routine, shows love her own way, and Reena, who takes these observations to a paediatrician.

subtype: Different ways of relating in toddlerhood [Actor]
passage: On the balcony, Avni sets her toy cars along the railing in a perfect row, red ones first. Zeenat, her aunt visiting from Lucknow, calls, "Avni, jaan, see the pigeons!" Avni does not look up. Zeenat's smile slips. Later Avni climbs into Zeenat's lap facing away and leans her whole back against her, humming one note. "That's her hug," Avni's father says. "She saves it for people she likes. The doctor sees her next month." Zeenat stays still and lets the humming go on.

qa.q: Which cars does Avni put first in her row?
qa.a: The red ones.

qa.q: How does Zeenat feel when Avni does not look up at her name, and what shows it?
qa.a: She feels a little hurt or disappointed; her smile slips.

qa.q: What choice does Zeenat make when Avni leans against her, and why does it help?
qa.a: She stays still and lets the humming go on, so Avni can enjoy the closeness her own way instead of being hugged the usual way.

qa.q: How does Avni's father see the back-lean differently from a visitor?
qa.a: He knows it is her kind of hug, saved for people she likes, so to him it is clear affection rather than distance.

grounding: It shows a toddler who lines up toys and responds less to her name yet shows love in her own way, with a doctor visit planned.

passage: In the colony sandpit, Ojas digs his own road right beside Rehana's castle, never touching it. He doesn't look at her, but he stays. "The blue bus goes from the market to the beach," he says, "and it has two doors, and the back door squeaks." Then he names every stop, in order, twice. Rehana pats sand onto her tower and listens. When her castle is done, Ojas quietly drives his toy bus right up to its gate and parks it there. "Bus stop," he says. Rehana grins. "Okay. My castle has a bus stop now."

qa.q: Where does Ojas park his toy bus?
qa.a: Right up to the gate of Rehana's castle.

qa.q: How does Ojas seem to feel about Rehana when he parks the bus at her castle?
qa.a: He seems friendly and eager to share his favourite thing with her, parking the bus at her gate even though he never looks at her.

qa.q: Which choice by Rehana kept the play going?
qa.a: She kept listening to the bus stops instead of walking off, and she welcomed the bus stop into her castle.

qa.q: How might Rehana see Ojas's play after the bus stop moment?
qa.a: She may realise he was playing with her all along, just side by side instead of face to face.

grounding: It shows a child who plays beside another child and talks at length about a favourite subject, and whose way of connecting is real.

passage: "Ammi, first teeth, then milk, then blue socks." "Shalini, today milk first. The van comes early." "No. Teeth first. Teeth, milk, socks." Her hands flap near her ears. Rehana kneels. "Okay, beta. Show me the chart." Shalini runs to the fridge and taps the picture cards. "Teeth. Milk. Socks. Shoes. Van." "Teeth it is. Super-fast teeth?" "Super-fast teeth." She brushes, gulps the milk, pulls on the socks. At the gate she tugs Rehana's sleeve. "Ammi, tomorrow is Saturday. Saturday chart is different. Saturday has park." "I know. You remind me." "I always remind you." She presses her cheek against Rehana's arm, once, then climbs into the van.

qa.q: What is the order on Shalini's morning chart?
qa.a: Teeth, milk, socks, shoes, van.

qa.q: Why does Shalini flap her hands when Rehana says milk first?
qa.a: The change to her set order upsets her; she needs the morning to go in the order she knows.

qa.q: What turning point in the morning made things go smoothly?
qa.a: Rehana asked to see the chart and followed it, making it a game with super-fast teeth instead of arguing.

qa.q: What would change if Rehana had insisted on milk first?
qa.a: Shalini would likely have become more upset, and they might have missed the van and the cheek-press goodbye.

grounding: It shows a child who needs a set order for the day and connects with her mother in her own real way.

passage: The report lay on the passenger seat, folded twice. Ojas didn't start the car. Was it the phone he had handed her at dinners? The late nights? The doctor had said, twice, that nothing he did caused it, but the question kept circling. In the back, Lavanya hummed and flicked the seat-belt buckle, click, click, perfectly happy. He watched her in the mirror and felt something fierce rise in his chest. Nothing about her had changed since morning. That evening he rang the number the therapist gave for a parents' circle. On Saturday a mother there showed him the card her son uses to ask for quiet, and Ojas took notes like a student.

qa.q: What was Lavanya doing in the back seat?
qa.a: She hummed and flicked the seat-belt buckle, click, click, perfectly happy.

qa.q: What was Ojas worried about as he sat in the car?
qa.a: He worried that something he did, like handing her the phone at dinners, had caused it, even though the doctor said it had not.

qa.q: What choice helped Ojas move from worry to support?
qa.a: He rang the number for a parents' circle and went to learn from other families, taking notes on practical ideas.

qa.q: How might Lavanya experience the day compared with Ojas?
qa.a: For Lavanya nothing changed; she was the same happy child, while the report shook Ojas.

grounding: It shows Ojas feeling guilt, worry and fierce love after learning Lavanya thinks differently, and then turning to other families and professionals.

passage: "The doctor said Inaya's brain works differently, Deepika, and I just nodded." "I nodded too, with my son. Then I cried in the lift." "Is it wrong that I'm angry? Not at her. At everything." "Not wrong. You're a good mother, Ayesha. It's worry with nowhere to go." In the next room, Inaya chatters to the buttons she is sorting into tins. "This morning she put a green button in my hand and walked off." "That's her hello. Mine brings me leaves." Ayesha laughs, eyes wet. "What do I do on Monday?" "Call the therapist I mentioned. Thursday, come to our parents' group. Tonight, let her sort buttons."

qa.q: What did Inaya put in Ayesha's hand?
qa.a: A green button.

qa.q: Why does Ayesha feel angry, according to the conversation?
qa.a: The news has left Ayesha worried and confused, and the worry has nowhere to go; the anger is not at Inaya.

qa.q: What small steps does Deepika suggest for the coming week?
qa.a: Call the therapist on Monday, come to the parents' group on Thursday, and let Inaya sort buttons tonight.

qa.q: What might it mean to Deepika to share the story of crying in the lift with Ayesha?
qa.a: It may feel like turning a painful memory into help; Deepika remembers how hard that news was and wants Ayesha to feel less alone.

grounding: It shows a parent's worry, confusion and love after learning her child thinks differently, and the help of another family and professionals.

subtype: Social rules that are not obvious [Actor]
passage: "Keerthana, hop to it!" Joseph Sir shouted across the ground. So Keerthana hopped, both feet together, all the way to the line. A few children laughed. Her cheeks burned. She had done exactly what he said. The drill went on, whistles and forty voices bouncing off the school wall, until her head felt packed with cotton. Joseph Sir didn't send her to stand in the corner. At the water tap he crouched to her level. "My mistake. 'Hop to it' is a saying. It only means come quickly. You weren't wrong to hop." Keerthana nodded slowly. "Can you just say come quickly next time?" "Deal. And if the whistles get too much, you can stand by the tap for a minute."

qa.q: What does Joseph Sir say 'hop to it' means?
qa.a: It only means come quickly.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel when the children laughed, and why?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and confused, with burning cheeks, because she had done exactly what he said.

qa.q: Which choice by Joseph Sir turned the moment around?
qa.a: Instead of punishing her, he explained the saying clearly and kindly, owned his mistake and offered a quiet spot by the tap.

qa.q: If Joseph Sir had sent Keerthana to the corner, what would change?
qa.a: She would learn that taking words literally gets her punished, and she would feel more ashamed and more tired, not less confused.

grounding: It shows a child who takes words literally and is worn out by school noise, helped by a clear, kind explanation instead of punishment.

subtype: Social rules that are not obvious [Actor]
passage: My name's Dhruv and I sit next to Charu, so I saw most of it. At break she walked straight into the middle of the skipping rope while Mitali's group was counting. The rope smacked her leg and they all shouted, "You can't just barge in!" Charu stood very still. Then she asked, "Where is that written?" They thought she was being cheeky. I don't think she was. She looked like she really wanted to know. Last period she had her head on her desk and her fingers in her ears, though only the fan was going. Ma'am saw and didn't scold. Next morning a card was pinned by the door: Skipping - wait at the end and ask, "Can I jump in?" Charu read it twice. At break she waited at the end of the line.

qa.q: What rule was written on the card by the door?
qa.a: Wait at the end and ask, 'Can I jump in?'

qa.q: How does Dhruv think Charu felt when she asked, 'Where is that written?'
qa.a: Dhruv thinks she was genuinely confused and curious, not cheeky, because she looked like she really wanted to know.

qa.q: What made the difference for Charu the next day?
qa.a: Ma'am wrote the unspoken rule down clearly instead of scolding, so Charu could read it and follow it.

qa.q: How might Mitali's group see Charu differently if someone explained what happened?
qa.a: They might see that Charu didn't know the unwritten rule, rather than thinking she was being rude or cheeky.

grounding: A classmate describes a child who finds playground rules confusing and is tired by school, and a clear explanation that helps more than scolding.

passage: Tuesday Dear Diary, Ishita didn't play dog-and-bone again. When the whistle went she walked to the far bench with her hands over her ears. Priyal said she's snobby. I don't think so. At lunch Ishita told me the whole route of the night train to Guwahati, every station, without stopping. I didn't understand half, but her eyes went shiny. So today I asked her, "Do you want to play something, or is the bench better?" She said, "Can we play trains?" We drew a timetable game in chalk. I was the passenger, she was the station master. Three more girls joined. Ishita laughed so loud! Tomorrow she's bringing her train cards. - Kavitha

qa.q: Which train's route did Ishita describe at lunch?
qa.a: The night train to Guwahati, every station, without stopping.

qa.q: What does Kavitha think about Priyal calling Ishita snobby?
qa.a: Kavitha doesn't agree and seems to think Ishita avoids the game for another reason, like the noise, not because she is proud.

qa.q: Which choice by Kavitha opened up a real friendship?
qa.a: Kavitha asked Ishita what she wanted instead of assuming, then played a train game built around Ishita's interest.

qa.q: How might Ishita see break time differently after the chalk timetable game?
qa.a: Break may feel like a place where she belongs, since others joined a game she loves and she laughed out loud.

grounding: A classmate notices a peer who avoids loud games and talks a lot about trains, asks instead of assuming, and includes her through her interest.

passage: During games period at the government school, some boys yelled "Train-wali!" as Pallavi slipped away from the noisy kabaddi circle. The new girl, Lalremsiami, watched her sit under the neem tree, counting on her fingers: engine, eleven wagons, guard van. Instead of guessing, Lalremsiami sat down a little distance away. "Do you want company, or quiet?" Pallavi thought. "Company. But no shouting." "Which train comes past here at four?" Pallavi's whole face opened. She explained the goods train with cement wagons and why it always waits at the signal. After school they stood at the level crossing and counted the wagons out loud together. Next day, when someone called "Train-wali" again, Lalremsiami said, "She knows more than the stationmaster," and kept walking beside her.

qa.q: What was Pallavi counting on her fingers under the neem tree?
qa.a: Engine, eleven wagons, guard van.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami seem to feel about Pallavi, and how can you tell she did not want to assume what Pallavi needed?
qa.a: She seemed curious and caring; she sat a little distance away and asked, 'Do you want company, or quiet?' instead of guessing.

qa.q: What turning point changed the teasing on the second day?
qa.a: Lalremsiami refused to join in, answered the teasing calmly and kept walking beside Pallavi.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel when Lalremsiami asks about the four o'clock train?
qa.a: Pallavi likely felt seen and happy; her whole face opened, and she gladly explained the goods train.

grounding: A classmate notices a girl who avoids loud games and talks about trains, asks instead of assuming, does not tease and builds friendship around her interest.

passage: All day at school Preeti ran her lines: raise the eyebrows when Tanya talks, say "No way!" at the right pause, laugh a beat after the others. She had written them in the back of her rough book. By the time the auto dropped her at the colony gate, her jaw ached. Inside, she didn't say hello. She dropped her bag, lay on the cool floor under the dining table and pulled her dupatta over her face. Nirmala, her mother, came from the kitchen, saw her, and asked nothing. She switched off the tube light, stopped the mixer halfway through the chutney and set a glass of water by Preeti's hand. An hour later a small voice came from under the table. "Mummy, can I just be weird this evening?" "Be exactly you," Nirmala said.

qa.q: Where had Preeti written her lines?
qa.a: In the back of her rough book.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel by the time she got home, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was drained and overwhelmed; her jaw ached, she didn't say hello, and she lay under the table with her dupatta over her face.

qa.q: Which choices by Nirmala gave Preeti a place to rest?
qa.a: She asked nothing, switched off the light, stopped the noisy mixer and left water nearby, then told Preeti to be exactly herself.

qa.q: How might the evening have gone if Nirmala had demanded to know what was wrong?
qa.a: Preeti might have shut down further or broken down, because she had no energy left to explain.

grounding: It shows a teenager who scripts expressions to fit in at school and shuts down at home, where acceptance lets her rest.

passage: "You were great at the fest, man. Everyone laughed at your jokes." "They weren't my jokes, Hemant. I practised them from a video. Forty times." "Seriously?" "And I watched how Rishi laughs and copied the timing. Head back, two seconds." "Why would you do that?" "Because when I laugh my way, people stare." Farhan pulls his hood over his eyes. "I've got nothing left. My face hurts from making faces." Ammi's voice from the doorway: "Farhan, the room's dark, the fan's on low. No dinner talk tonight unless you want it." "Thanks, Ammi." "Should I go?" Hemant asks. "Stay. Just don't need me to talk." "Fine by me. I'll read. And you don't have to do the Rishi laugh here." A snort comes from under the hood: Farhan's own laugh, crooked and short.

qa.q: How many times did Farhan practise the jokes?
qa.a: Forty times.

qa.q: Why does Farhan copy Rishi's laugh?
qa.a: He is afraid of being stared at, because when he laughs his own way, people stare.

qa.q: What choice helped Farhan rest after the fest?
qa.a: Ammi kept the room dark and quiet with no dinner talk, and Hemant stayed without needing him to talk.

qa.q: What is it like for Hemant to learn the jokes were practised?
qa.a: Hemant is surprised, since the fest looked easy for Farhan, but then understands and offers him a place to be himself.

grounding: It shows a teenager who copies peers' scripts and laughs to fit in and is exhausted afterward, with acceptance at home giving him rest.

passage: Forty minutes before judging, the extension cord died and the science-fair model went dark. Vasudha, who had built the circuit, went silent, eyes on the floor. Mohit had seen others snap, "Look at me, what's wrong?" He didn't. He crouched beside the table, not too close, and spoke slowly. "The lights are off. I think it's the cord. Do you want to say it, or write it?" The hall buzzed; the loudspeaker crackled. He slid a pair of earmuffs across the table. "My sister's. Use them if you want." Vasudha put them on. Ten long seconds passed. Mohit waited. Then she tore a strip of chart paper and wrote three steps. Mohit did them one by one. At the third step, the little street lamps on the model flickered back on.

qa.q: What went wrong forty minutes before judging?
qa.a: The extension cord died and the science-fair model went dark.

qa.q: Why did Mohit not tell Vasudha to look at him?
qa.a: He seemed to understand that forcing eye contact would add stress, and he wanted her to answer in her own way.

qa.q: Which of Mohit's choices helped most under time pressure?
qa.a: He spoke slowly, asked if she wanted to say or write it, offered earmuffs and waited, so she could give clear steps.

qa.q: How might Vasudha have felt if Mohit had snapped at her like others?
qa.a: She might have frozen further in the noise and not been able to share the fix she knew.

grounding: It shows a teen who speaks clearly, gives time, respects sensory needs, avoids forcing eye contact and asks how she prefers to communicate.

passage: Before the colony Holi, Swati heard that the new boy in C-block, Pranav, didn't like being touched. On the morning itself she saw him at the edge of the park in big headphones, watching the dhol from far away. Her friends were already running at him with fistfuls of pink. "Wait," Swati said, stepping between them. She stopped an arm's length off and didn't try to catch his eye. "Happy Holi. Colour, or no colour?" He said nothing. She waited, counting drumbeats. Finally he held out his phone. He had typed: No colour. Gujiya yes. "Gujiya coming," she said, and went to fetch a plate. When she came back, he had moved one step closer to the party. He typed again: You can text me. It's easier.

qa.q: What did Pranav type the first time?
qa.a: No colour. Gujiya yes.

qa.q: What does Pranav moving one step closer suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt safer and more welcome once Swati respected his space and his answer.

qa.q: What was the key choice Swati made when her friends ran at Pranav?
qa.a: She stepped between them, stood back, asked instead of assuming, and waited for his answer.

qa.q: If you were Pranav, what would you want from the other children at Holi?
qa.a: I would want them to ask first, not throw colour or grab me, and to let me answer by text if that is easier.

grounding: It shows a teen who respects sensory needs and personal space, gives time to answer and learns how another person prefers to communicate.

passage: Every Thursday at seven, Nkechi set up the moth trap in the university garden in Manchester: same corner, same white sheet, same flask of rooibos. When a girl from her building, Hana, wandered over and said, "Cool light," Nkechi answered, "It's a special lamp for moths, and please don't stand on the sheet." Hana stepped back, laughing. "Fair. What have you caught?" Nkechi talked for twenty minutes about the elephant hawk-moth: its pink wings, the way its caterpillar pretends to be a snake. Hana didn't seem to mind the lecture. The next Thursday she arrived at seven exactly, with her own flask and a sketch. "I drew the hawk-moth." Nkechi studied it. "The antennae are wrong. The rest is good." Hana grinned. "Then show me."

qa.q: What did Nkechi drink at the moth trap every Thursday?
qa.a: A flask of rooibos.

qa.q: What does Hana arriving at seven exactly suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she enjoyed Nkechi's company and the moths, and wants to share the interest and respect the routine.

qa.q: Which choice by Hana turned a blunt answer into a friendship?
qa.a: Hana laughed and asked a question instead of taking offence, then came back with her own sketch.

qa.q: How might another student see Nkechi's comment about the antennae?
qa.a: Someone else might find it rude, but Hana sees it as honest help and a way to learn more.

grounding: It shows a young adult with a deep passion, direct speech and a steady routine, whose honesty and focus draw in Hana, who comes to share the interest.

passage: The hostel common room was loud with the TV, so Lakshmi read in the stairwell, as she did every night from nine to ten, headphones on, a photocopy of a temple inscription on her knees. Rajni from Room 14 sat two steps below with her history assignment. "You're the inscriptions person, right? Could you check this?" Lakshmi read it once. "Your second paragraph is wrong. That grant is Chola, not Pallava. The rest is fine." Rajni blinked, then laughed. "Okay, blunt. Thank you." "I'm not being rude. You asked." "I know. It's actually useful." Lakshmi showed her how to spot the older letter shapes, and the hour vanished. At ten sharp, Lakshmi stood up. "Same time tomorrow? Quiet only." "Quiet only," Rajni agreed.

qa.q: Where does Lakshmi read every night from nine to ten?
qa.a: In the stairwell, because the common room is loud with the TV.

qa.q: Why does Lakshmi add, 'I'm not being rude. You asked'?
qa.a: She seems to worry her direct answer might be taken badly and wants Rajni to know she meant it as honest help.

qa.q: What made this conversation grow into a friendship?
qa.a: Rajni accepted the blunt feedback as useful, and they bonded over the inscriptions while keeping Lakshmi's quiet routine.

qa.q: How does Rajni see Lakshmi's directness by the end of the evening?
qa.a: Rajni sees it as useful and honest, and happily agrees to Lakshmi's quiet-only rule.

grounding: It shows a young adult with a deep interest, direct speech and a need for quiet and routine, whose honesty helps a new friendship form.

passage: By eleven each morning, Jagdish was already tired. The open-plan floor at the Bengaluru office rang with phones and chatter, and every coffee trip meant small talk about weekend plans he didn't have. The work itself he loved. Give him a messy dataset and a clear question, and he would vanish into it for hours. The trouble came with messages like "Make the report more punchy." On Friday he wrote to his manager, Manoj: "I work best with written tasks and a clear definition of done. Could I also use the quiet room in the afternoons?" Manoj replied within the hour. "Of course. I'll put tasks in writing from Monday. Tell me what else helps." Jagdish read it twice, then leaned back and let out a long breath.

qa.q: What did Jagdish ask to use in the afternoons?
qa.a: The quiet room.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel after reading Manoj's reply, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt relieved; he read it twice, leaned back and let out a long breath.

qa.q: What turning point improved Jagdish's working week?
qa.a: He clearly asked in writing for written tasks, a definition of done and use of the quiet room, instead of struggling silently.

qa.q: How might Manoj see the request from a manager's side?
qa.a: Manoj seems to see it as reasonable and useful, since clearer instructions help Jagdish do the work he is good at.

grounding: It shows an adult drained by open-plan noise, small talk and vague requests, who thrives with clear written tasks and feels relief when an adjustment is granted.

passage: "So Saturday. Maybe brunch, maybe the market, we'll see how we feel?" Sonali said, stirring her tea. Ishita put her cup down. "Can I tell you something about 'we'll see'?" "Uh oh." "No, it's fine. When plans are open like that, I spend the whole week running every version in my head. By Saturday I'm tired before we leave the flat." "I didn't know that." "I didn't say it before. I thought it would sound strange. But you're my closest person, and I'd rather you know." Sonali was quiet, then pulled a notepad from the drawer. "Okay. Saturday. Brunch at eleven. Market after, one hour. Home by three. Better?" "Much better." Ishita laughed, a little shakily. "Thank you for not calling it silly." "It isn't silly. Now I actually know how to plan with you."

qa.q: What time did Sonali write down for brunch?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: Why did Ishita not mention the problem with open plans before?
qa.a: She thought it would sound strange and was worried about how Sonali would react.

qa.q: What choice made the Saturday plan work for both of them?
qa.a: Ishita explained her need honestly, and Sonali wrote down a clear plan with times instead of leaving it open.

qa.q: How does Sonali's view of their weekends change after the talk?
qa.a: Sonali now understands why open plans tire Ishita and finally knows how to plan with Ishita.

grounding: It shows an adult for whom unclear plans are draining, who asks for a clear plan in a close relationship and feels relief at being understood.

passage: Every reading hour at the village school, Parul slid the Hindi reader under her mat. The letters jumped about; ब and व looked like twins, and d and b swapped places in English too. "I'm stupid," she whispered to herself. But at home she fixed Dadaji's radio by watching how the wires ran, and she could repeat every story her cousin Simran told, word for word. One evening Simran read aloud while Parul followed with her finger. When Parul stumbled, Simran didn't sigh. "Your brain is quick, Parul. Only this part is hard. We'll go slow." The next week Simran went with Parul's mother to ask the teacher about extra reading help, before the school year ran on.

qa.q: What did Parul fix at home?
qa.a: Dadaji's radio, by watching how the wires ran.

qa.q: What does Parul's whisper 'I'm stupid' show about how she sees herself?
qa.a: It shows she has started to believe she is not clever because reading is hard, even though she is bright.

qa.q: Which choice by Simran protected Parul's confidence?
qa.a: Simran read slowly with her without sighing, told her that her brain is quick, and helped arrange early help at school.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Parul if Simran had not spoken up?
qa.a: The teacher might think Parul was lazy or careless for hiding the reader, and miss that she needs reading help.

grounding: It shows a bright child who stumbles over letters, hides her reader and thinks she is stupid, and patient early help that protects her confidence.

passage: On library day in the Cardiff school, Daniel always chose the thickest dinosaur book, then pushed it to the back of his cubby. The words swam. He mixed up "was" and "saw" and lost his place every line. But in the maker corner he built a working drawbridge from craft sticks and string before anyone else had finished their plan. Ms. Mina, the reading specialist, found the dinosaur book behind his lunch box. She didn't scold. She sat beside him with a coloured reading strip. "You figured out that drawbridge with no instructions," she said. "That's a strong brain. Reading is just a different puzzle for it. Want to try one page together?" Daniel laid the strip under the first line. Slowly, he read about a stegosaurus.

qa.q: What did Daniel build in the maker corner?
qa.a: A working drawbridge from craft sticks and string.

qa.q: Why might Daniel hide the dinosaur book in his cubby?
qa.a: He seems embarrassed and worried because the words swim and he loses his place, so he hides that reading is hard.

qa.q: What was the turning point when Ms. Mina found the hidden book?
qa.a: She didn't scold; she pointed to his strength, offered a reading strip and read one page with him.

qa.q: How might Ms. Mina see Daniel after the drawbridge and the hidden book?
qa.a: Ms. Mina likely sees a bright, capable builder who finds reading hard, not a lazy child, and believes one page together can help.

grounding: It shows a bright child who mixes up words and hides books, and a patient adult whose early help keeps his confidence.
